transcript: Welcome to the stone Aron of Agira, a surviving witness to the town’s medieval Jewish heritage.
Its pointed arch may remind you of a doorway. But this structure had a different purpose.
An Aron ha-Qodesh is the sacred ark of a synagogue: the place where the Torah scrolls are kept. These scrolls contain the five books of Moses and hold a central place in Jewish religious life.
The Aron of Agira originally belonged to the synagogue in Via Santa Croce. It is dated to fourteen fifty-four and is recognised as one of Europe’s oldest surviving stone synagogue arks.
Take a moment to look at its carved details: the pointed arch, the decorated capitals, and the horizontal band bearing Hebrew letters.

These features belong to a sacred furnishing made for a community that gathered here to worship. The stone preserves a tangible connection to that community, centuries after the synagogue ceased to serve its original purpose.
The Hebrew inscription is a key to understanding the Aron.
It draws on a verse from the Book of Isaiah, chapter two, verse five:
“O house of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the Lord.”
These words connect the structure directly to the sacred text. They also provide the basis for its dating.

Hebrew letters can carry numerical values. The interpretation of marked letters in this inscription identifies the Jewish year five thousand two hundred and fourteen, conventionally given in the sources as fourteen fifty-four.
Time has worn the inscription, making parts of it difficult to read. Its study therefore required more than an examination of the surviving stone.

After visits beginning in nineteen ninety-five, the scholar Benedetto Rocco established its dating in nineteen ninety-six. The local historian Filippo Maria Provitina assisted him, and an old photographic glass plate helped recover portions of the inscription that had become less legible.
An earlier image had preserved what the stone was gradually losing.
The inscription allows us to recognise this structure as a sacred ark and to place it within the history of the medieval synagogue.
The Aron once stood in the synagogue of Via Santa Croce, serving the Jewish community of Agira.
Its original setting changed after the expulsion of the Jews in fourteen ninety-two. The former synagogue became a Christian place of worship, known as Santa Croce.

Within that later setting, the stone structure framed a Christian altar. Its appearance could be understood as an architectural surround, while its Hebrew inscription preserved evidence of its earlier purpose.
The Aron was eventually transferred and reassembled in the Church of the Most Holy Saviour, the Santissimo Salvatore.

Its survival allows us to encounter a part of the town’s history that might otherwise be difficult to see. The community that commissioned it left behind more than a date: it left an object made to protect its sacred writings.
As you look at the Aron, remember its original function. This was the place where Torah scrolls were kept, within a synagogue used by the Jewish people of the town.
Today, the surviving stone helps keep the memory of that community present.
